neutral_facts.value: The accused, who was a resident of Nagenahalli village, was searching for the victim's house on the day of the incident. He met a witness who directed him to the victim's house. The accused informed the victim that he had come with 'S', the son of her brother, and asked if 'S' had arrived. The victim stated that 'S' had not come. Later, the victim did not visit the house of a neighbor to watch TV as usual because she had relatives in her house and had to cook for them. The next day, the victim was found murdered. The investigating officer arrived at the scene, and a fingerprint expert found the accused's fingerprint on a plastic cover at the scene. The accused was arrested six days later, and blood-stained clothes and a steel rod were seized. The accused's blood group matched the victim's, and the steel rod was found at the scene. However, the investigation was criticized for not properly examining the blood stains on the steel rod and for not conducting a test identification parade.

quotes.text: Allowing the appeal, the Court HELD: 1. The High Court proceedeq on the basis that the case was one of circumstantial evidence.

prosecution_argument.value: The prosecution argued that the appellant went to the house of the victim-deceased and robbed her ornaments and murdered her. The High Court relied on the circumstances that the appellant was found in the deceased's house on the fateful day, his fingerprint was found on a plastic cover, his clothes were blood-stained and matched the blood group of the deceased, the ornaments of the deceased were recovered at the instance of the appellant, and the weapon of offence was discovered at the instance of the appellant.

quotes.text: The prosecution case was that on 5th November, 1990, the appellant who was resident of Nagenahalli village was searching for the victim-deceased house.

defence_argument.value: The defence argued that the High Court's reliance on probabilities was insufficient, as there was no evidence about the appellant's whereabouts from 1 P.M. to 8.30 P.M., no TIP was held, and the fingerprint identification was shrouded in mystery. The trial court's acquittal was a plausible view and the High Court should not have upset it.

quotes.text: The view taken by trial court giving appellant the benefit of doubt was certainly a plausible view and in the absence of any perversity in the view taken, the High Court ought not to have upset the conclusion.

legal_principle_applied.value: In a case of circumstantial evidence, there has to be some degree of trustworthiness and certainty about the existence of the circumstances; mere probabilities are certainly not enough.
